title: What the four tools do
narration: A coronary angiogram uses four tools that do different jobs. The sheath gives the team a way in. The guidewire helps direct equipment. The catheter carries contrast, and the contrast makes the heart’s arteries show up on X-ray.
visual_direction: Begin with a simulated coronary tree filling, then reveal the episode title. Show a short sheath, a slender wire, a long hollow catheter and a contrast syringe in that order. Keep brand and product names off the tools.

title: Two routes, the same goal
narration: The team can enter an artery at the wrist or the groin. We’ll follow a right wrist example. The catheter travels through connected arteries to the aorta, the large artery that leaves the heart. The groin route reaches the same area from below.
visual_direction: Reuse the approved radial and femoral arterial geometry from Episode 01. Mark both entry sites. Reveal a palm-up right wrist at the thumb side, then trace the wrist and groin paths separately inside the arteries. Both terminate in the aortic root.

title: The short access wire
narration: At the numb wrist, the team places a fine needle into the artery. In this example, a short access wire passes through the needle. The needle comes out and the wire stays in place. That short wire helps the team put the sheath into the artery.
visual_direction: Reuse the validated wrist cutaway, with the vessel inside the thumb-side forearm. Show the short access wire appearing from the needle tip into the open arterial channel. Withdraw the needle fully while the short wire remains. End on the short wire at the wrist.

title: The sheath stays at the entry site
narration: The sheath is a short, hollow tube. It goes in with a tapered insert that helps it enter. The insert and short wire come out, leaving the sheath at the wrist. It gives the team a passage to move a catheter in or out without making another puncture there.
visual_direction: Keep the preceding wrist orientation. Animate sheath and tapered insert together around the stationary short wire. After they reach the vessel, withdraw the insert and short wire, leaving the outer sheath fixed. Hold an enlarged section of the empty passage. Use no measurements or hand placement.

title: How groin access can differ
narration: At the groin, the team may use a finer wire and a temporary tube before placing the working sheath. The steps and equipment can vary. Once the working sheath is in place, it serves the same purpose as at the wrist.
visual_direction: Visually switch to the right common femoral artery using the earlier femoral cutaway. Use two brief states from the existing proof: fine wire with the temporary introducer, and the working sheath after exchange. Use a labelled time jump so they cannot be mistaken for a direct swap or a continuous animation. Return to the wrist in P06.

title: The long diagnostic guidewire
narration: Back at the wrist, a longer guidewire goes through the sheath. Live X-ray, called fluoroscopy, helps the cardiologist see it travel through the arteries. The thin, flexible diagnostic catheter slides over that wire toward the aorta near the heart. The sheath stays at the wrist.
visual_direction: Start with the longer wire moving through the stationary sheath. Use the established body map for travel and a small cutaway showing the catheter wrapped around the wire, with the wire tip ahead. End with both in the aortic root above the aortic valve. Keep the short access wire off screen.

title: The guidewire comes out
narration: Near the heart, the cardiologist withdraws the long guidewire from the catheter. The catheter stays in place. The team positions its curved tip at the opening of a coronary artery, just above the aortic valve. The wire is out before the contrast injection.
visual_direction: Continue from the aortic-root geometry. Pull the long wire back completely through the catheter while the catheter remains stable. Then seat only the catheter tip at the left coronary opening. Keep the tip shallow and the lumen open. Hold a full beat with neither wire nor contrast visible before P08.

title: Contrast outlines the artery
narration: The team injects a liquid called contrast through the hollow catheter. As it mixes with blood and moves through the coronary artery, it makes the channel inside the artery visible on X-ray. The outline fades as the contrast moves on with the blood.
visual_direction: Animate contrast exclusively through the catheter lumen, out of the tip at the left opening, then into the left main and downstream branches. Match the flow to a grayscale X-ray simulation in the same projection, with dark contrast filling the lumen. Fade it from the image during washout. Show no contrast at the sheath.

title: When the X-rays are recorded
narration: The team records a short series of X-rays while contrast is flowing, so the pictures show the arteries filling. They can move the X-ray camera for another view. They position the catheter at the other coronary opening for a separate injection and set of pictures.
visual_direction: Make the recording indicator appear only during the contrast run. Let the X-ray arm change angle between short runs. Preserve the left system projection within its run. Cut to a separate right coronary injection with the catheter at the right opening, and let that run fill and fade independently. Do not depict the change as a continuous catheter exchange.

title: What to tell your care team
narration: Before the test, tell the team about kidney problems or any past reaction to X-ray contrast. The contrast usually contains iodine. Some people feel briefly warm during an injection. If you feel unwell, especially if you have chest discomfort, itching or trouble breathing, tell the team right away.
visual_direction: Use a quiet consultation illustration with icons for kidneys and prior contrast reaction. Then show the patient talking to a staff member in the cath lab. Keep the prior-reaction prompt about contrast and present brief warmth separately from symptoms to report. Skip drug, volume and treatment details.

title: How the tools work together
narration: Once the test is finished, the team removes the catheter and sheath and checks the entry site. The sheath provided a passage, the guidewire guided the catheter, and the catheter delivered the contrast. The moving X-rays are what the cardiologist reviews next.
visual_direction: Begin with the catheter withdrawing through the still-seated sheath, then withdraw the sheath and show the wrist compression band. Close on the four matching opener illustrations beside a short simulated angiogram loop. Save findings and image interpretation for the next episode.
